clue.text: Speculate on artist representative of us

indicators.note: in an across answer, one thing placed on another comes after it, so the speculation part follows the artist

blocks.note: Augustus John, the Welsh painter
to bull is to speculate on a rise in share prices

explanation.surface: A gallery owner gambles on a painter who seems to stand for all of us.
explanation.walkthrough: A bull on the Stock Exchange buys hoping prices will rise.
explanation.definitionFit: John Bull is the stock cartoon figure personifying England and the English people, so he stands for the British 'us'.

clue.text: Some travellers suffer from this delay - put a spurt on

indicators.note: putting one thing on another in a down answer places it above, so the spurt sits on top of the delay

blocks.note: a jet is a sudden spurt of liquid or gas
a lag is a delay or interval

explanation.surface: Travellers held up by a delay are urged to hurry along.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the opening descriptive phrase; the wordplay sits after the dash, with 'on' meaning above in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Jet lag is the tiredness long-haul air passengers feel after crossing several time zones quickly.

clue.text: Could be badly hurt in such an accident

definitions.text: Could be badly hurt in such an accident

blocks.clueFragment: Could be badly hurt in such an accident
blocks.note: surface reading: a warning about injuries in some kind of mishap
setter's reading: the kind of road accident where a driver strikes someone and then drives away

explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly hurt in' tempts you to look for an anagram, but there are not the right letters; the whole clue simply describes the accident.
explanation.definitionFit: A hit-and-run is a collision where the motorist strikes a pedestrian and flees, often leaving the victim seriously injured.

clue.text: Coach top person for performance in a way

blocks.note: a coach is a long-distance bus
the king is the person at the top

explanation.surface: A sports coach seeks out the leading player for a performance of sorts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way' here means a street or road, so the performance happens out in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: Busking is playing music or entertaining in the street for coins from passers-by, a show staged in a public road.

clue.text: Street lighting once provided for those driving along coast

definitions.text: provided for those driving along coast

blocks.note: first meaning: torches carried through dark streets in former times

blocks.clueFragment: provided for those driving along coast
blocks.note: second meaning: seaside golf courses, where golfers drive the ball

explanation.surface: A note on old street lamps put up for motorists on a coast road.
explanation.walkthrough: The drivers are golfers, not motorists.
explanation.definitionFit: Links were pitch torches carried by link-boys to light streets; links are also coastal golf courses where players drive off tees.

clue.text: Stars dont shine when examined

blocks.note: first meaning: the constellation also called the Big Dipper
second meaning: old British slang for failing an exam

explanation.surface: Stars that fail to twinkle when someone looks at them closely.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Stars' a plural subject, but it is the name of a star group, and the rest is the slang verb meaning to fail a test.
explanation.definitionFit: The Plough is the British name for seven bright stars in Ursa Major; to plough is dated slang for failing an examination.

clue.text: Showing tolerance that's new in period of abstinence

indicators.note: something in a period sits inside it, so these letters go within the fast

blocks.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting before Easter
i.e. abbreviates id est, 'that is'
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone is surprisingly forgiving during a stretch of self-denial.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenient is an adjective for being mild and forgiving, which matches showing tolerance towards others.

clue.text: Like a rough diamond found in a foreign nick

blocks.note: un is French for 'a'
a nick is a small cut

explanation.surface: A rough diamond turns up in a prison cell abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' suggests a British slang word for prison, but here it is a small cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough diamond has not yet been shaped by a gem cutter, so it is literally not faceted or polished.

clue.text: Highly confidential - still gets duplicated

indicators.note: duplicated means written twice, so the same word is set down two times side by side

blocks.note: hush means be still or quiet
the same word written a second time

explanation.surface: A top-secret document is still being photocopied.
explanation.definitionFit: Hush-hush is informal for secret, describing matters kept very quiet and shared with very few people.

clue.text: In accord with amendment of harsh laws

indicators.note: an amendment changes a text, so the letters before it are rewritten in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A legislator agrees to a change in some severe legislation.
explanation.definitionFit: Draco was the Athenian lawgiver whose code was famously severe, so draconic describes punishing, strict legislation like his.

clue.text: Awfully industrious-can't play

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the letters are jumbled out of their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone very hard-working who is unable to have any fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' reads as a verb about leisure, but it is the noun: a work by Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Titus Andronicus is Shakespeare's early revenge tragedy, so it is a stage drama.

clue.text: For instance, include loose women within extended family

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it inside, so the first piece wraps around the second

blocks.note: 'as' introduces an example, as in 'such as'
to loose a knot is to untie it

explanation.surface: Relatives are told to count, say, promiscuous women among the wider clan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose women' looks like one phrase, but 'loose' is a verb and 'women' starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Aunties, an affectionate form of aunts, are female relatives outside the immediate household of parents and children.

clue.text: Top-class sprinter - one said to take drugs, perhaps?

indicators.note: said means spoken, so we want a word that is pronounced like the description that follows

blocks.clueFragment: one said to take drugs, perhaps
blocks.note: an athlete who takes drugs is a cheater, in British speech with no final r

explanation.surface: An elite runner is rumoured to be doping.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'perhaps' marks drug-taking as one example of cheating.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheetah is the fastest land animal, reaching about seventy miles an hour in short bursts.

clue.text: Guides using sign on trail

indicators.note: in an across answer, one piece placed on another comes after it

blocks.note: to drag is to trail along the ground
an omen is a sign of what is to come

explanation.surface: Trackers follow markers left along a path.
explanation.definitionFit: Dragomen were interpreters and guides employed by travellers in Arabic, Turkish and Persian speaking countries.

clue.text: Threatening a Conservative minister at first

indicators.note: at first tells us the preceding word is placed at the front rather than read in clue order

blocks.note: Min. is an abbreviation for minister or ministry
taken as written
a Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A Tory minister was menacing from the outset.
explanation.definitionFit: Minatory is a formal adjective meaning menacing, expressing or conveying a threat of harm.

clue.text: Leaders in this influence many eminent statesmen

definitions.text: Leaders in this influence many eminent statesmen

indicators.note: leaders are the front runners, so the first letter of each following word is kept

blocks.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: Editorials in this very paper sway powerful politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders' are also newspaper editorials, and 'this' is the paper the puzzle appeared in, so the whole clue describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Times, the newspaper printing this puzzle, has long had editorials read and heeded by politicians and the establishment.

clue.text: Model made by author of horse, not quite finished

indicators.note: not quite finished means stopping just short of the end, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: Thomas Mann, the German novelist
equine means of or relating to horses

explanation.surface: A sculpture of a horse by a writer, left incomplete.
explanation.definitionFit: A mannequin is a dummy, or a person, used to display clothes, so it is a fashion model.

clue.text: This guide our railways had was complicated

indicators.note: something complicated is tangled, so these letters are mixed up

blocks.note: BR is British Rail, the national railway in 1993
these six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A timetable for Britain's trains was a notoriously confusing read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our' points to the British setter's own national railway.
explanation.definitionFit: Bradshaw's Railway Guide was the famous Victorian timetable listing every train service in Britain.

clue.text: How to raise standards? Athlete uses this approach

blocks.note: first meaning: hoisting flags up a pole
second meaning: the sprint before a jump or throw

explanation.surface: Tips on improving performance, with a sportsman's method as example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standards' sounds like quality levels, but here they are flags.
explanation.definitionFit: To run up a flag is to hoist it; a run-up is the approach run a jumper or bowler takes before the action.

clue.text: Carriage taking hard-hearted father to school

indicators.note: having something as a heart means holding it in the middle, so it goes inside the next word
adding one thing to another joins the next piece on after it

blocks.note: H is the pencil-lead abbreviation for hard
pa is an informal word for father
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: A stern father is driven to school in a horse-drawn coach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard-hearted' looks like a single adjective for a cruel father, but it means H in the heart of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A phaeton is a light, open four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage, popular in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

clue.text: Poisonous stuff put into blend, in particular

indicators.note: to blend is to mix, so the letters of the word before it are stirred into a new order
put with in at the end means placed inside, so the mixed letters go within the last word

blocks.note: these four letters rearranged
nice can mean fussy or particular, as in a nice distinction

explanation.surface: Something toxic is added to a mixture, especially.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' reads as a preposition but supplies the letters to be mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicotine is the toxic alkaloid found in tobacco, used historically as an insecticide and deadly in large doses.

clue.text: Didn't eat a lot of nuts

blocks.note: first meaning: picked at one's food, as in 'she barely ... her dinner'
second meaning: slightly mad

explanation.surface: Someone only nibbled at a big bowl of nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of nuts' looks like one phrase, but the split comes after 'lot', and 'nuts' means crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who only touched their meal ate little of it; touched is also informal for slightly crazy or unbalanced.

clue.text: Sounds like appropriate contributor for Spectator

indicators.note: sounds like says we want a word pronounced the same as the next one, not spelt the same

blocks.note: to appropriate is to take for oneself, to steal

explanation.surface: A suitable writer for a magazine, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as the adjective 'suitable' but is the verb meaning to take.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Steele co-founded The Spectator with Joseph Addison in 1711 and wrote many of its essays.

clue.text: Unfriendly? Certainly not immediately approachable

blocks.note: first meaning: cool and aloof in manner
second meaning: far away, so it takes time to reach

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves seem to describe a standoffish person; the second is literal, about something far off.
explanation.definitionFit: Distant describes a reserved, cold person and also a place a long way off that cannot be reached quickly.

clue.text: Approach game cautiously as bridge player, say

blocks.note: South is one of the four players at bridge
to say something is to talk

explanation.surface: A card player creeps up warily on the next game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like a card game but means hunted animals; bridge players are named North, South, East and West.
explanation.definitionFit: To stalk is to creep quietly towards wild animals being hunted, staying unseen until close enough.

clue.text: Source of power turned off — that could be wise

indicators.note: a source is where something begins, so only the opening letter of the next word is used
off suggests something gone wrong or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the first letter of power
taken as written

explanation.surface: Switching off the electricity supply might be a sensible move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned off' reads as one phrasal verb, but 'turned' is the fodder and 'off' the signal to mix it.
explanation.definitionFit: Prudent means showing careful good judgement about the future, a close synonym of sensible and wise.

clue.text: Top artist covers up swindle in gallery

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece that covers another sits on top of it

blocks.note: PRA is the President of the Royal Academy, the senior British artist
to do someone is to cheat them

explanation.surface: A leading painter hides a fraud in an art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers up' suggests hushing up a scandal, but it just places one piece above the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The Prado in Madrid is Spain's national art museum, holding works by Velázquez, Goya and El Greco.

clue.text: Play bringing anguish to audience in theatre

blocks.note: heartbreak is overwhelming grief
the house is the theatre audience, as in a full house

explanation.surface: A drama that leaves its theatregoers distraught.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartbreak House is George Bernard Shaw's 1919 drama, so it is a stage work for the theatre.

clue.text: Welsh agreeing to meet in English town

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for Welsh
to OK something is to approve it, so OKing is agreeing to it

explanation.surface: People from Wales consent to a meeting in an English location.
explanation.walkthrough: Woking is a commuter town in Surrey, south-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Woking is a sizeable Surrey town, a place in England in the London commuter belt.

clue.text: Make short work of prisoner of limited intelligence

blocks.note: con is short for convict
dense means slow-witted

explanation.surface: Someone deals swiftly with a dim-witted inmate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make short work of' is an idiom for dealing quickly with something; the definition is only its first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To condense a text is to shorten it, reducing its length while keeping the substance.
